before: **William Wadé Harris** was a Liberian of the Grebo people. After a time in prison, he reported a vision that called him to preach. In 1913 and 1914 he traveled along the coast of what is now Côte d'Ivoire and into what was then the Gold Coast, and today is Ghana, carrying a Bible and a cross. He called people to burn their idols, to give up evil practices and to be baptized. Large numbers responded. He did not found a large church of his own at first. He urged people to join the churches of the missions, and the Methodist and other mission churches in the region grew greatly after his visit. Colonial authorities in Côte d'Ivoire arrested and expelled him in 1914. A church that looks to him as its founder, the Harrist Church, exists today.

**Garrick Sokari Braide** was an Anglican in the Niger Delta of Nigeria. Beginning in about 1915 he preached repentance and prayed for the sick, and crowds followed him. The colonial government arrested him in 1916, and he died in 1918.

**Simon Kimbangu** was a believer in the Belgian Congo who had some connection with a Baptist mission. In 1921 he began praying for the sick, and large crowds came. The Belgian authorities arrested him after a few months, and he was imprisoned until his death in 1951. A church that follows him, the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth by the Prophet Simon Kimbangu, exists today.

before: In South Africa, a different pattern appeared. The American healing ministry of John Alexander Dowie in Zion, Illinois, influenced early groups that came to be known as Zionist churches. before: The Church of Pentecost in Ghana began with the work of James McKeown, an Irish missionary sent by the Apostolic Church of Great Britain. He arrived in the Gold Coast in 1937, at the invitation of a Ghanaian prayer-and-healing group led by Peter Anim. After disagreements in the following years, McKeown and the congregations that followed him separated in 1953 from the mission that had sent him, and in 1962 the Ghanaian body took the name Church of Pentecost. Under Ghanaian leaders it grew into one of the largest churches in Ghana, with missionaries going out to other nations. The story shows that foreign and local leaders both mattered, and that conflict about authority may occur even among faithful people.
